## Event-Driven Azure AD Sync

Cutting identity sync latency from 30 minutes to seconds — without touching the default sync interval.

AI-designed · Infrastructure-executed · Zero AI at runtime

## The Problem

By default, Microsoft Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) synchronizes Active Directory changes to the cloud every 30 minutes . For environments where identity changes need near-instant propagation — onboarding, access control, compliance — that delay is unacceptable.

The common fix? Reduce the sync interval to 5 minutes or less. But that means polling 6x more often , burning CPU on the AD server and the sync engine, even when nothing changed.

30m

Default sync interval

5m

Typical "fix" (polling)

<10s

Our approach (event-driven)

## The Solution

Instead of polling harder, we let the OS tell us when something matters. A Windows Scheduled Task listens for Security Event IDs — the exact signals Windows emits when AD objects change — and fires a delta sync only when needed.

🖥️

AD Change

User created,
password reset, etc.

→

📋

→

⚡

instantly

→

Entra ID

## Monitored Events

The task watches for 13 Security Event IDs covering the full lifecycle of user and group changes:

4720 User created

4722 User enabled

4723 User info changed

4725 User deleted

4726 User disabled

4738 Global group created

4728 Added to global group

4729 Removed from global group

4732 Added to security group

## Implementation

A lightweight helper script on the Domain Controller handles the sync call:

# C:\_sync.ps1

Import-Module 'C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure AD Sync\Bin\ADSync\ADSync.psd1'

Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta

The Windows Scheduled Task Auto-EntraSync-OnADChange runs as SYSTEM with a 10-minute execution limit, registered via XML to ensure reliability over remote management.

The default 30-minute sync cycle remains intact as a safety net — the event trigger is an acceleration layer, not a replacement.

## CIS Benchmark Compliance Auditor

60 security controls evaluated in 6.3 seconds — automated, read-only, risk-prioritized.

AI-built · Deterministic at runtime · Zero AI inference during scans

## The Problem

Manual CIS Benchmark compliance audits are slow, repetitive, and easy to deprioritize — leading to security gaps going undetected. Audit policies sit at "None" for months. Password policies drift from baseline. Without regular automated checks, the gap between what the benchmark requires and what the environment actually enforces grows quietly.

This is especially critical for Domain Controllers, where a single misconfiguration can expose the entire directory to credential theft, relay attacks, or unauthorized access.

## The Approach

Built an automated, read-only compliance auditing tool:

🐍

⚡

9 data categories

PowerShell collector pulls live DC configuration across 9 data categories: password policy, audit policy, user rights, registry values, services, firewall, time sync, LSA settings, and security options.

Python comparison engine evaluates collected state against 60 CIS Level 1 controls defined in a JSON ruleset — no code changes needed to add or modify controls. The engine runs entirely on deterministic rule matching; no AI model is called during scan execution, which is why results are fast, consistent, and fully reproducible.

Report generator outputs a risk-prioritized remediation report (Critical → High → Medium → Low) with plain-language explanations and specific GPO paths for each finding.

The tool is read-only — it does not make configuration changes. Remediation remains a reviewed, manual step.

Key findings: 6 Critical failures (password complexity, LM auth level, firewall, LSA settings). Audit Policy at 0% pass rate (9/9 failed) — no logging coverage for credential validation, Kerberos auth, directory service access, or account management.

System hardening without audit logging is blind — you can't detect what you don't log.

## Validation

To verify the automation's time-saving claim, a representative sample was manually audited: all 9 Audit Policy controls plus all 6 Password Policy controls (15 of 60 total), using standard tools ( secpol.msc , Group Policy Management Console) cross-referenced against CIS Benchmark documentation.

Manual verification took 22 minutes — a best-case baseline measured with an experienced operator and a pre-prepared checklist. A first-time audit without prior familiarity would take meaningfully longer.

Automated scan: 6.3 seconds for all 60 controls.

v2 will extend the JSON-driven ruleset to cover Azure AD / Entra ID CIS controls, requiring no code changes to the core engine. The same architecture applies: collector pulls cloud tenant state via Graph API, comparison engine evaluates against Entra ID-specific benchmarks, report generator outputs the same risk-prioritized format.

Entra ID CIS Benchmark Audit — v2 | AppoSight Use Cases



## Entra ID CIS Benchmark Audit — v2

The v1 CIS auditor, extended from on-prem to the cloud tenant — deterministic, read-first, reproducible. And an honest record of where the platform drew the line.

AI-executed · Human-verified · Self-correcting on error

## The Problem

The v1 CIS auditor covered the on-prem Windows side — 60 controls on a Domain Controller via WinRM and PowerShell. It said nothing about the cloud: Microsoft Entra ID, where identities, MFA, Conditional Access, and privileged-access controls actually live in a hybrid setup.

v2 extends the same JSON-driven, deterministic engine to the tenant. Instead of PowerShell over WinRM, the collector pulls live tenant state from the Microsoft Graph API using a service principal, and the same comparison engine evaluates it against Entra ID / CIS controls — no code changes to the core, and no AI model invoked during the audit. What follows is the real result of that audit on a Microsoft 365 Developer Program tenant : what the platform let us read, what it let us fix, and where it refused the write.

## Results — Verified, Not Claimed

Final state of the remediated Developer Program tenant, re-read from the live API after each write. Green changed as intended; red blocked at the platform tier.

2 → 0
Weak MFA methods (Email + TAP) enabled

no → yes
FIDO2 attestation enforced

0 → 0
Conditional Access policies (platform-gated)

off → off

Users with a registered MFA method

## Technical Note — the Developer-Tenant Platform Tier

A distinct, reusable finding about how Microsoft 365 Developer Program tenants expose Conditional Access. This is a different kind of ceiling from the P1/P2 feature-level restrictions (PIM, Identity Protection) — and it matters for anyone building or testing automation against Developer tenants.

API surface Developer Program tenant Commercial / paid tenant

CA policy read GET conditionalAccessPolicies 200 (empty list) 200

CA policy write POST conditionalAccessPolicies 403 "not licensed" 201

MFA method flags PATCH authenticationMethodsPolicy 204 204

Registration-enforcement PATCH registrationEnforcement 400 "invalid" 204

PIM / Identity Protection (P2-gated) AadPremiumLicenseRequired licensed

Two separate ceiling classes:

Feature-level (P1/P2): the entire capability is absent until licensed — PIM, Identity Protection, PIM-eligible roles. These return AadPremiumLicenseRequired and are simply not evaluated ; there is no write surface to probe.

Platform-tier (CA + registration-enforcement): the API surface exists and is readable in a Developer tenant, but the write path is gated by tenant class. The read succeeds (200); the write is refused (403 for CA, 400 for registration) — a licensed-capability gate on the mutation , not an absence of the feature.

Takeaway This is a genuine platform constraint on the Developer Program tier — not a scope, consent, or payload problem (all three were ruled out by isolation probes). It is reported as a platform ceiling, not as an "assign a license" remediation.

## Case Study

Three findings, in the order they were discovered. Every number below was verified from the live tenant (re-read after each write), not from intent.

## a. MFA Method Hardening — applied & verified

The free-tier MFA method configuration is writable in a Developer tenant, and this fix landed and persisted — PATCH authenticationMethodsPolicy returned HTTP 204 , confirmed by a follow-up read.

Method Before After

Email enabled disabled

TemporaryAccessPass enabled disabled

FIDO2 isAttestationEnforced false true

MicrosoftAuthenticator enabled kept

SoftwareOath enabled kept

SMS / Voice disabled already off

Effect: the two most phishable strong-auth methods (email one-time code, 6-hour TAP) are off the tenant; any completed MFA must be app- or certified-hardware-backed.

## b. The P2 Assumption Error — caught & corrected

An earlier pass of this audit recommended two fixes that assumed a paid/licensed capability was provisionable in a no-license Developer tenant — until challenged to verify the claim against live tenant data:

"C2 — Zero Conditional Access policies → Fix: publish CA policies (free-tier, available now)" · and the PIM / Identity Protection items as "assign P2 (free-tier, no trial)".

That was incorrect. This is a Microsoft 365 Developer Program tenant ( subscribedSkus = [] , assignedLicenses = 0/23 ) — it cannot provision P1/P2 at all (no trial, no self-serve subscription). The read API for P2-gated features still works; the write / activation path is gated by tenant class — the same split documented in the technical note above.

How it was caught:

The license inventory was empty before any fix was written — subscribedSkus: [] , 0/23 user licenses assigned. The "assign P2" fix had nothing to assign.

The write probes returned 403 / 400 , not success — the first signal this was a gate, not a payload bug.

The read-vs-write contrast — CA GET → 200 while CA POST → 403 under the same scoped token — proved a tenant-class gate, not a scope / consent problem.

Lesson On Developer Program tenants, probe the write once before promising it. P2-gated features are "not evaluated — requires a license (unavailable in this tenant)"; CA-policy creation and MFA registration-enforcement are "attempted — blocked at the platform tier (403/400)"; only free-tier, unlicensed configuration is reliably writable. Do not restate a licensed feature as a "free, available-now" fix.

## c. The CA / Registration-Gate Discovery — attempted, blocked, root cause identified

Two items could not be remediated in this tenant, with the exact responses:

MFA registration-enforcement (C1 gate): PATCH authenticationMethodsPolicy → registrationEnforcement…state = active → HTTP 400 "The configured RegistrationEnforcement is invalid." Retried on v1.0 and beta across four payload shapes — consistently rejected.

Conditional Access policy creation (C2): POST conditionalAccessPolicies → HTTP 403 "Your tenant is not licensed for this feature. Please upgrade your subscription." Retried with enabled , disabled , and minimal-body variants — consistently rejected.

Root cause: both are licensed capabilities the Developer Program tier does not expose for writes. Not scope (the token carried Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess / Policy.ReadWrite.AuthenticationMethods ), not consent (admin-consented), not payload (multiple shapes). A platform-tier gate.

Hybrid AD ↔ Entra Onboarding / Offboarding | AppoSight Use Cases ## Hybrid AD ↔ Entra Onboarding / Offboarding A deterministic, role-driven pipeline that onboards and offboards employees across on-prem Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID — with human checkpoints for the judgment calls, and a complete, honest audit trail. Automation does the bulk · Humans own the judgment calls · Every step audited ## The Problem Onboarding and offboarding a hybrid employee is slow and error-prone because the steps span two identity systems plus mail, device, and delegation surfaces that are easy to miss. The most common failure is incomplete access removal on offboarding — a disabled account that still holds group memberships, active sessions, MFA methods, shared-mailbox delegates, or third-party OAuth tokens. On the other side, onboarding is inconsistent: the same role gets a different set of groups depending on who typed the commands, and there is no record to prove it happened. The fix is a deterministic, role-template-driven flow where AD is the source of truth , the deterministic bulk is automated, the judgment calls are explicit human checkpoints, and every step — including every failure — is written to a timestamped audit log. ## The Architecture On-prem Active Directory is the write path. Azure AD Connect syncs changes to Microsoft Entra ID. Microsoft Graph is used read-only to verify state and drive the audit — never as a second write source, so the two systems never disagree. WRITE AD account + group membership ──(WinRM, DC)──► on-prem AD BRIDGE Azure AD Connect (delta sync) ───────────────► pushes AD → Entra ID VERIFY Microsoft Graph (read-only service principal) ► confirm + audit CONTROL explicit human checkpoints — logged, never auto-approved Role templates drive assignment. Nothing privileged or irreversible is auto-executed. ## Results — Measured, Not Claimed Both flows were run end-to-end against a real hybrid lab (on-prem AD, Azure AD Connect, Microsoft Entra ID) for a test employee, and every number below was read from the timestamped audit of that run. 7 / 7 Role groups assigned on onboarding (verified in AD) 9 Groups removed on offboarding (incl. nested) 30 Timestamped audit events, offboard run 4 Human checkpoints (offboard) — all logged, none auto-approved ## Where the time actually went A single known lab defect dominates the wall clock: the AD Connect sync-trigger cmdlet hangs (~90 s per run, finding F4). Stripping that one hung call out, the real automation work is small and fast: Operation Measured Note Onboard — account + 7 groups + Entra verify ~37 s 95 s wall includes one 90 s sync-trigger hang Offboard — disable, pw reset, 9 group removals ~12 s 92 s wall includes one 90 s sync-trigger hang 9-group removal (the critical step) < 1 s / group via Set-ADGroup -Remove ; the Remove-ADGroupMember cmdlet hung (F2) Manual baseline — an estimate, clearly labelled A skilled operator doing the same ~20 steps manually across AD + Entra + mail consoles typically takes 30–45 minutes per offboard, with a real risk of missing a group, MFA method, OAuth token, or delegate — and no trace that it happened at all. This baseline is an estimate, not a stopwatch run ; the automation's real value is completeness, auditability, and determinism, not raw speed. ## The Findings — Where the Platform Drew the Line These are the non-obvious, verified-in-lab facts that any team building this automation will hit. Reported honestly — not hidden as errors. Finding What happened UPN suffix is not assumed An AD account [redacted] synced to Entra as [redacted] — not the expected domain. All Entra lookups therefore key on onPremisesSamAccountName (reliable), never the guessed UPN. Group-removal cmdlet hangs Remove-ADGroupMember hung indefinitely in this multi-DC lab, while the delta-attribute path Set-ADGroup -Remove @{Member=…} completed all 9 removals in < 1 s/group. The pipeline uses the working path and a hard per-call timeout as the guard. Session contamination A hung WinRM op left the shared WSMan session locked, so every following call returned HTTP 400. Fixed by evicting the session on timeout so the next call opens fresh — after which the group assignments succeeded. Disabling ≠ revoking OAuth revokeSignInSessions returned 403 (scope not granted to the service principal). Disabling an account does not by itself invalidate third-party "Sign in with Microsoft" tokens — the scope must be granted and the call made. Developer-tenant limits No Exchange, no Intune, 0 subscribed SKUs, 0 dynamic groups. So mail delivery, shared-mailbox delegates, Intune wipe, and the license- conflict branch could not be exercised — each is logged as a valid negative result, not a silent skip. The takeaway The hard part of identity automation is not the happy path — it is the failure modes and the platform's quiet limits : a cmdlet that hangs instead of erroring, a shared session that poisons itself, an OAuth revocation that 403s, and a Developer tenant that can't host the mail/device surfaces you expect. An honest audit surface all of these; a happy-path script hides them. ## What Was Not Exercised (Stated Explicitly) Final account deletion — gated behind IT + HR dual sign-off and a legal-hold check; intentionally not executed in the demo (the safe default). The code path is present. Shared-mailbox / SharePoint delegate removal — no Exchange/SharePoint in the lab; the check runs and is logged, but real removal is untestable here. Intune device wipe / unenroll — no enrolled devices; the flag-then-decide path is present, but no destructive action was taken (no auto-wipe by default). Third-party OAuth revocation — blocked by the 403 scope; not validated end-to-end. License-conflict resolution branch — only the "no conflict possible" path was hit (0 SKUs / 0 dynamic groups); the overlap-resolution path is untested. Multi-UPN-suffix tenants — only a single-suffix on-prem domain was tested. See also: Entra ID CIS Benchmark Audit — v2 → · Event-Driven Azure AD Sync →

Deploying a Domain Controller to Azure with an AI Agent | AppoSight



## Deploying a Domain Controller to Azure with an AI Agent

How an AI agent extended our on-premises Active Directory into the cloud — provisioning, networking, and validating a new domain controller with a human approving every credentialed step.

## The goal

As a sysadmin managing on-prem Active Directory (two Windows Server domain controllers, already hybrid-synced to Microsoft Entra ID), we set out to test a practical question: could an AI agent handle real, end-to-end infrastructure deployment — not a scripted demo, but actual cloud provisioning, networking, and Active Directory work — while a human stayed in control of every sensitive step?

The project: deploy a new, additional domain controller in Azure that joins and replicates with our existing on-prem domain. Nothing on-prem was removed or replaced — this was extending our AD environment into the cloud, coordinated through an AI agent with terminal, SSH, and browser-automation access.

An isolated, no-uplink clone of one domain controller was created early on as an additional safety measure. In practice, most of the networking and troubleshooting work took place directly against the production environment — a real, live infrastructure test, with every privileged or potentially destructive action requiring explicit human execution rather than agent autonomy.

Result: a fully functioning, replicating domain controller running in Azure, verified with zero replication errors across all three domain controllers, in both directions.

## The architecture

Component
Details

Azure Resource group with a VNet, network security groups locked to a single trusted IP, a VPN Gateway supporting both site-to-site and point-to-site connectivity, and a Windows Server 2022 VM

On-prem Existing KVM host running the two production domain controllers, an isolated test network used for early validation, and strongSwan providing the IPsec tunnel

Connectivity A site-to-site VPN tunnel carrying only traffic between the on-prem subnet and the Azure VNet, with every AD-relevant port (Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, RPC, SMB) explicitly allowed and everything else denied

## What the agent actually did

Provisioning went the way automation should: the AI agent handled Azure CLI work directly, built the VNet, subnets, NSGs, VPN Gateway, and VM, and caught several of its own mistakes along the way — an invalid package name, a misconfigured firewall rule, an Azure capacity wall on the first VM size requested. In each case it diagnosed the actual error text and adjusted rather than guessing blindly.

The real test, though, was what happened once the infrastructure existed but the new domain controller still couldn't properly talk to the rest of the domain. Getting from "VM exists" to "VM is a healthy, replicating domain controller" required finding and fixing three genuinely subtle network faults — the kind that don't show up in a checklist and don't have a single obvious cause.

## Fault 1 — A tunnel that was "up" but carried no traffic

The VPN tunnel reported a healthy, connected state on both ends. But pings and connection tests across it failed 100% of the time. Rather than assume the tunnel itself was broken, the agent checked its actual encryption counters directly and found them frozen at zero — meaning no real traffic had ever crossed it, despite the healthy status.

Tracing further, it found the on-prem host's own firewall was silently rewriting the source address of outbound traffic before the tunnel's encryption policy could ever match it — so packets bound for Azure were losing the very identity the tunnel needed to recognize and encrypt them. The fix was a single, precisely ordered firewall exception. Verification wasn't just "no more errors" — the agent re-checked the same encryption counters and watched them move from zero to real traffic before calling it fixed.

## Fault 2 — Traffic worked one way, but not the other

With the tunnel actually carrying data, on-prem-to-Azure connections worked — but Azure-to-on-prem connections were explicitly rejected, not merely timing out. That distinction mattered: a timeout would suggest a routing gap, but an explicit rejection meant something was actively firing.

The agent traced the exact firewall rule evaluation order and found the inbound rule required a connection to already be "established" — a condition no brand-new connection can ever satisfy. The outbound-direction rule had no such restriction, which explained the asymmetry perfectly. This same bug reappeared once, after a routine reboot regenerated the firewall configuration with the broken rule instead of the fix — so the agent didn't just patch it again, it rewrote its own recovery script to verify the rule's position and correctness , not merely its presence, closing the gap for good.

## Fault 3 — The hardest: a silent packet-size mismatch

This was the hardest problem of the project. Small operations across the tunnel — DNS lookups, short authentication exchanges — worked perfectly. But the domain controller promotion process itself, which requires larger network exchanges, would hang for ten-plus minutes and fail with an unhelpful, generic Windows error.

The agent worked through this methodically: ruling out clock synchronization (a real but insufficient earlier fix), confirming the tunnel's actual usable packet size was smaller than either side assumed, and finally identifying that Windows was sending packets larger than the tunnel could carry — with the network's standard "please shrink your packets" signal being silently dropped rather than delivered. This is a notoriously difficult class of network fault precisely because it produces no useful error message at all.

The fix required a kernel-level rule rewriting oversized packets down to a safe size at the tunnel boundary. What stands out here is the verification discipline: the agent's first attempt to confirm the fix used an indirect signal, and it explicitly declined to accept that as proof. It then built a direct, unambiguous test — and in doing so caught a second , more subtle bug: the fix's own matching rule excluded exactly the packets that needed rewriting. It corrected that too, and only declared the issue closed after a counter-based test showed 41 out of 41 relevant packets crossing at the corrected size, with zero at the old, broken size.

## Making it durable

Once all three faults were fixed, the agent noted — unprompted — that none of the fixes would survive a reboot, since they existed only in the running system's memory. It built a dedicated boot-time service to reapply them automatically, carefully avoiding a trap it identified in advance: naively enabling the system's default firewall service would have wiped out unrelated rules for other services running on the same host.

This wasn't just claimed to work — a real, full reboot was performed, and every fix was confirmed present and correctly ordered afterward, with the tunnel automatically reconnecting and full connectivity restored without any manual intervention.

## Where the human stayed in control

Three categories of action never left human hands, for the entire project:

Credentials. Every password — host access, domain administrator credentials, VPN certificates — was entered interactively by the human or scoped through narrow, read-only permissions the agent could use without ever seeing a secret.

The domain controller promotion itself. The single command that actually made the new server a domain controller was run manually and live by the human, every time — including through genuine unrelated failures (a stale process lock, a corrupted internal database state) that had nothing to do with the network work and needed independent troubleshooting.

Privileged network changes. Every firewall and routing modification was staged by the agent as a reviewable script and executed by the human — which had the added benefit of leaving a clean, auditable trail of every change made.

## Verified outcome

repadmin /replsummary

Source DSA largest delta fails/total %% error
CONTO-DC 28m:30s 0 / 10 0
CONTO-DC2 32m:59s 0 / 10 0
vm-w2022-poc 23m:12s 0 / 10 0

Destination DSA largest delta fails/total %% error
CONTO-DC 23m:12s 0 / 10 0
CONTO-DC2 21m:24s 0 / 10 0
vm-w2022-poc 33m:00s 0 / 10 0

Zero replication failures, in both directions, across all three domain controllers — confirmed live, in an active session on the newly deployed Azure domain controller.

Azure Portal’s auto-generated resource dependency view for the deployment’s resource group

## What this actually demonstrates

The interesting result isn't that an AI agent can run a single well-documented promotion command — it's that, given real infrastructure access and a disciplined human-in-the-loop model, it performed genuinely hard systems debugging: correlating symptoms across firewall rule order, packet captures, and kernel networking behavior; distinguishing a real fix from one that only looked correct; and knowing when to stop and hand a step back to a human rather than push through.

Equally important is what it never did. Across dozens of privileged operations, the agent never held a production credential, never executed an irreversible domain change unsupervised, and — when a password was accidentally exposed mid-project — flagged it for rotation immediately rather than proceeding as if nothing had happened. That boundary wasn't added afterward. It was the operating model from the first message, and it held for the entire project without exception.

See also: Auditing and Securing a Domain Controller on Azure →

Upgrading a 2× Windows Server 2019 Domain to Server 2025 — Full Technical Case Study | AppoSight



## Upgrading a 2× Windows Server 2019 Domain to Server 2025 — Full Technical Case Study

A two-phase swing migration with a strict stop-and-report discipline.

Environment (sanitized): a lab/POC Active Directory forest contoso.example on a single KVM/Ubuntu host (NAT bridge 192.0.2.1/24 ). Two Windows Server 2019 domain controllers, an identity-sync service, and one operator working over remote management with a strict stop-and-report discipline. Timeline: a two-phase swing migration — a clean, verified sequence, then the rename/re-IP identity saga. Names below are placeholders for the real hostnames, accounts, and IPs. No credential values, password policies beyond "the domain minimum length", or storage locations for secrets are included by design.

This case study demonstrates supervised execution, not autonomous reliability — the AI agent supplied speed and breadth, while the human operator held the gate, the snapshot, and the independent read-back. That split, not the tool, is what made the migration survivable.

Reading note. This is deliberately written as a narrative, not a log. The dead ends — the theories that were wrong — are included because they are the most transferable part of the story. Every claim here was cross-checked against the project record; where the record itself was corrected over time, the corrected version is the one told here.

The bottom line, for a skimming reader. This case study is a demonstration of supervised execution, not autonomous reliability . An AI agent drafted every step — but the thing that kept this forest alive was never the agent. It was the human operator: a strict stop-and-report gate before every mutation, a snapshot behind every one of them, and an independent read-back from a second vantage after each. The agent supplied the speed and the breadth; the operator supplied the judgment. That split — speed from the machine, authority from the human — is the transferable point, and it is the one most worth copying. The technical detail below is the evidence for it.

## 1. Summary

Starting state. One domain, two Windows Server 2019 domain controllers (dc-01 at 192.0.2.2 holding all five FSMO roles, dc-02 at 192.0.2.3), forest and domain functional level at the 2016 generation, DFSR-based SYSVOL, and a dormant identity-sync (ADSync) agent living on the primary DC.

End state. Two Windows Server 2025 domain controllers — dc-03 (192.0.2.4, all five FSMO roles + global catalog) and the rebuilt second DC (192.0.2.2, global catalog; this box reclaimed the original primary DC's identity after a clean rebuild — see §5). Forest and domain functional level raised to Windows 2025 . Identity sync moved off the DCs to a dedicated member server, member-sync-01 (192.0.2.6). The two 2019 DCs were demoted, powered off, and retained (not deleted) as rollback material.

Duration. The clean part of the job — pre-flight, schema prep, two new DCs, FSMO transfer, sync-service move, decommission of the old DCs, functional-level raise — was a straightforward sequence of verified steps. The second half, the rename-and-re-IP phase and the DC4 identity saga, produced the project's most valuable lessons.

## 1.5 Lessons Learned (the transferable set)

The one-place summary for a reader who will not read the rest. Each is framed as a general principle, not a project-specific directive:

In-place identity changes on stateful infrastructure create effectively unenumerable rollback surfaces. Identity lives in registries, caches, SPN stores, replication topologies, DNS zones, and directory objects; you cannot enumerate the writers in advance, so the rename/re-IP phase cost the project a long stretch of elimination work. Build with the final names from the start instead (§5, §6.1–6.2).

Stateful "fresh" operations can silently reuse existing state. Promotions re-attached to a stale, pre-existing damaged directory object, and the box's local copy won every merge by sequence number — three demote/re-promote cycles later, the fix was to verify the created object , not the command's success . Read whenCreated / objectGUID after every promotion (§5, §6.3).

The completion gate is an independent, time-gapped read-back of intended final state — never the command's success line. Two "verified" successes here silently removed nothing ; the pattern that caught both was a second, independent read on the authoritative vantage, gapped in time. The action token is truth; the prose summary is not (§4.11, §6.5).

Name and DNS churn is a first-class failure surface. The sync-failure loop, the stale-record cleanup, and the unresolved forwarder contradiction were all downstream of identity churn. DNS state belongs in the read-back gate of every mutation, not in afterthoughts (§6.4).

Self-modifying artifacts on critical systems are standing risks, not historical ones. A scheduled task that could demote a DC — armed, on-demand-allowable, with a past-due schedule — was a live gun in the domain. "Next Run Time: N/A" is not safety (§4.9, §6.7).

Ambiguous infrastructure error strings must be verified against ground truth before a theory is built on them. "Failed to get write lock" was actually a security-policy file-open denial; the kernel audit log decided it in one read, and the wrong theory cost a full session (§4.6, §6.8).

Interactive confirmation prompts are a hidden failure class over stdin-less remote sessions. Blocked prompts orphan processes that hold write locks, and the orphans stack until read-only queries jam. Mutating writes that confirm interactively belong on an interactive console (§3.7, §4.10).

Full detail: §6 ("What I'd do differently") carries the project-specific reasoning behind each; the numbered items above map to it.

## 2. Approach and method

Five rules governed every state change, from the first step to the final rebuild:

Clean install + swing migration, not in-place upgrade. The 2025 DCs were built as new VMs and brought up alongside the healthy 2019 DCs; roles were handed over, then the old boxes were demoted. The forest never dropped below a healthy DC count by design — though, as §5 shows, the rename phase still found a way to break that rule briefly.

Snapshot before every state change. Every mutation — schema prep, join, promotion, demotion, rename, IP change, FL raise — was preceded by a disk-only hypervisor snapshot, retained as a rollback point (34+ snapshots across the VMs at closeout). This discipline is what made recovery possible throughout; two of its limits (a snapshot-revert state restriction and a snapshot-became-live-disk trap) are cataloged in §4.

One DC at a time. A new DC was not declared done until it was fully verified — replication in both directions, services, identity — before the next one started.

Stop-and-report gates. Each state-changing step required explicit operator authorization, was executed, and was independently verified before the next step. Multiple "success" reports during the project turned out to be false (§4, false-success entries); the gate that mattered was always the read-back, not the exit code.

Read-only verification before acting. Suspicious readings (a schema "anomaly", replication error codes, "join is broken" signals) were cross-checked with a second method before anyone touched anything.

## 3. Timeline by phase

## 3.1 Pre-flight (read-only) → GO

Verified read-only before any change was authorized: replication healthy (0/5 failures both directions, all partitions), DFSR running on both DCs (a hard prerequisite — the old FRS was absent), functional levels at the 2016 generation, all five FSMO roles on dc-01, time sync healthy, storage headroom confirmed. Baseline snapshots were taken on both 2019 DCs — the first of the snapshot-everything discipline.

Two things to note from this phase:

Replication noise that recurs all project: every repadmin /replsummary showed a lone 110 (enumeration timeout) line. That is normal repadmin query noise in a healthy forest, not a replication failure. It was flagged early because it kept looking alarming later.

No backup engine existed. The first "Windows Server Backup" attempt hung silently because wbadmin resolved to the GUI applet ( wbadmin.msc ) in a non-interactive remote session — the backup feature was disabled on both DCs and the engine binary was absent. Decision: rely on the hypervisor disk snapshots (restorable, satisfies the checkpoint rule) rather than enable a backup engine that would require reboots.

## 3.2 Schema preparation

Run on the schema master with the 2025 media mounted, as a service account that had been (reversibly) added to Schema Admins.

forestprep hung at 0% CPU. The adprep tool presents an interactive "type C to continue" prompt; over a remote-management session with no interactive stdin, the read blocks forever. Fix: pipe the answer in ( echo C | adprep.exe /forestprep ). Result: RC=0, schema advanced three versions (baseline objectVersion = 88 → 91), verified on both DCs, replication still 0/5.

A false alarm, properly handled. The intended baseline check first queried a non-existent attribute and mis-read the schema naming-context head object's class ( dMD ), producing an apparently abnormal reading. The schema NC head legitimately has objectClass = dMD — standard, expected. The correct, authoritative check ( objectVersion on the schema NC head) returned a clean baseline consistent with the 2016 functional level. No change to AD was needed; the "anomaly" was a measurement error. Lesson: verify an abnormal AD reading with a second, independent method before acting.

gpPrep syntax error: /gpprep run standalone returns RC=1 — it must be paired with /domainprep . The corrected combined invocation returned RC=0 (idempotent skip). Phase 1 closed fully verified.

## 3.3 Building the new DCs

Provisioning. Each new DC was a peer of the working 2019 boxes: 2 vCPU / 8 GB, same bridge, 60 GB disk. The unattended install failed in two distinct, evidence-diagnosed ways before succeeding:

Firmware re-injection. Stripping the boot loader from the VM definition was not enough — the hypervisor metadata and an SMM element re-injected UEFI firmware on every re-define, while the answer file was authored for legacy MBR. The answer file was rebuilt for the legacy firmware and the final state was verified against the live hypervisor process command line, not the defined XML.

Zero-byte disk writes. Setup read the media but wrote 0 bytes to the disk — diagnosed with block-statistics (media read > 0, disk write bytes = 0): the answer file had no driver for the paravirtualized block device. Fix: present the disk on the same bus type as the working 2019 peers (SATA), matching what was known to work.

First-boot networking failure, a self-inflicted regression, and a clean revert. The first fresh install booted to a healthy lock screen but never got an IPv4 address (full-capture evidence: zero DHCPv4 DISCOVER packets). The wrong first fix attempt — merging a static IP into the Windows registry offline , onto two guessed adapter GUIDs — produced a corrupt TCP/IP profile that crashed the guest on network-stack init. Reverting surfaced a hypervisor limitation : snapshot-revert refused the disk-snapshot state outright ("Invalid target domain state 'disk-snapshot'. Refusing"), so the revert was done manually — destroy the VM, move the bad thin overlay aside for forensics, re-point the domain's system disk at the clean base image, re-define, start. The box recovered; the operator then set the IP inside the guest , where it belonged. Lesson recorded: for a fresh install with an unmapped NIC, in-guest configuration is faster and safer than offline registry surgery.

Domain join. Verified from the other DC's vantage (the reliable one): the AD computer object showed the new FQDN and service principal names — fields written only by a successful join. Multiple "join is broken" signals (empty Domain= , token-cache errors, blank secure-channel reads) turned out to be artifacts of probing inside a SYSTEM-privileged remote session, not a failed join — cross-checked and dismissed.

Promotion blockers, in the order hit (full index in §4): cmdlet parameters that no longer exist on the 2025 build; the DSRM password having to satisfy the domain password policy (the domain's hard maximum caps the length — a too-short candidate was rejected as "too short" and an overly long one as "too long", which is how the cap was discovered); a UTF-16LE-encoded script that cmd.exe cannot parse (silent no-op — the process started and never ran ); a blocking console-read over a stdin-less remote session; rapid remote-session churn producing HTTP 500s; a stale-file false positive (the "file exists" check was validating an abandoned earlier variant — the fix was to hash-verify the exact file before launch); and finally the real wall — a credential realm mismatch : the promotion scripts had been building the domain-qualified account name with a wrong realm spelling , which makes the KDC reject the ticket (error 1825) and DC discovery fail (error 1908). Network, DNS, secure channel, and privileges all looked fine — the exact signature of a realm mismatch. Correcting the realm (or using the unambiguous UPN form) was the operator's diagnosis, and with it the promotion completed.

Result. First 2025 DC promoted, verified (replication 0/5 both directions, global catalog, all core services running), and — per the one-at-a-time rule — work stopped for sign-off before the second box. The second DC followed the same proven path. Two benign DNS-delegation warnings on each promotion (expected in a root forest with no parent zone) were recorded and closed.

## 3.4 FSMO transfer

With both 2025 DCs promoted, replicating, and one holding the global catalog, all five FSMO roles were transferred to dc-03 (the new primary) — operator-authorized, then independently verified from both DC vantages that all five roles sat on dc-03 and that replication remained 0/5. Notably, one earlier cleanup attempt on the second DC (an identity scrub) had been reverted by a reboot — the reboot itself proved the root cause (a registry-level identity source re-painting the old name on every registration), which became a key lesson and a recurring theme of §5.

## 3.5 Identity-sync (Entra ID Connect) move (tracked separately from the DC phases)

The dormant ADSync agent on the primary 2019 DC had to come off the DC (sync services belong on a member server, and the DC was about to be demoted). This phase had its own failure cluster:

The uninstaller family of failures. The standard uninstall path repeatedly "succeeded" while leaving the product behind: the MSI engine hung on the agent's packages (four stalls across sessions); completed uninstalls left orphan Uninstall registry keys ; the agent's components were live services sharing install directories , not dormant files — deleting files under a running service changed nothing. The eventual reliable pattern: enumerate the services and their image paths first ; stop → verify they stay stopped → disable → delete the service — then remove files and registry entries; and use direct key/file removal once the standard uninstaller had wedged twice, because retrying a wedged uninstaller is how the cycle continued.

Completion signal discipline: "the process is gone" is not done. Done = registry key absent + install directory gone , verified read-back.

The new member server, member-sync-01 , was built as a peer of the DCs, joined, and the sync service installed and tested — after which a first full sync completed and the service went live. The dormant agent on the old primary was then fully removed to zero (services stopped and deleted, orphan keys removed, verified absent).

## 3.6 Decommissioning the 2019 DCs

Second 2019 DC (dc-02): demoted, verified (no longer a DC from the domain's vantage; replication clean with the remaining set), powered off, retained . Demotion over the remote channel required a parameter the old docs never mentioned (the local-admin seed that suppresses a silent console prompt); omitting it made the demote hang with zero AD DS activity — a wedged demote with no AD DS events means nothing happened : kill, re-verify full-DC state, retry.

First 2019 DC (dc-01): same staged sequence. One twist worth recording: the demote completed (RC=0) even with a wrong-but-present local-admin seed value — the parameter is a prompt-suppression/re-provision seed, not a credential-checked gate; presence unblocks, the value is not validated. Verified by domain-side evidence (DC count, DC-list membership, SRV records), not the box's own self-report.

Both 2019 DCs: demoted, shut off, retained — no autostart, so the host could not resurrect them; disk images and all their snapshots kept as rollback material.

## 3.7 Functional-level raise — the last irreversible step

Forest and domain functional level raised to Windows 2025 — the irreversible final step, gated on both live DCs being 2025.

The WinRM lesson: Set-ADForestMode / Set-ADDomainMode are hang-prone mutating AD writes — the interactive confirmation over a stdin-less remote stream blocks, and every client-side timeout leaves an orphaned remote PowerShell on the DC holding an AD write lock; those orphans stack , and eventually jam even read-only AD queries. The operator therefore ran both raises from the interactive console , where they completed cleanly on the first try — no orphans, no lock-jam. Independent verification from both DC vantages (functional levels read back, replication 0/5, FSMO stable, sync service healthy, all core services running) closed the entire 2019→2025 migration.

Rule carried forward: long-running AD DS writes belong on a console/RDP session, not over a remote channel with short client timeouts. And the completion gate is always the live read-back, never the command's success line.

## 3.8 Phase 6 — rename and re-IP the 2025 DCs onto the original identities

Goal: give the second new 2025 box the original dc-01 identity (192.0.2.2) and settle the naming. Operator-confirmed method: netdom computername (the supported path for a DC identity change — not Rename-Computer , which doesn't handle DC identity/SPN/DNS), then the IP change, each preceded by a snapshot and a stop-and-report gate.

This phase is where the project got hard, and where the record is most honest about itself. In order:

A failed rename attempt and a full rollback to the clean snapshot — including a host/hypervisor-level finding that applied to all future work on the host (below).

The hypervisor/AppArmor wall. The VM that had gone through an undefine / define cycle refused to start with a misleading "Failed to get write lock" error. The first working theory — an orphaned kernel file lock — was tested against evidence and formally withdrawn (a libvirtd restart did not clear it; a full device/inode/lock scan found no lock holder anywhere; a non-blocking lock test acquired the "locked" file successfully as the hypervisor user). The ground truth was the kernel audit log: AppArmor was denying a plain read of the VM's base disk, because the per-domain AppArmor profile for this one VM included a .files fragment that did not exist — the profile body was stale (its mtime predated the whole crisis), and the VM's XML disk-chain listing was truncated, so the allowlist did not cover the real backing chain. The fix was surgical and scoped: rebuild the XML to the full disk chain, create the missing .files fragment mirroring a healthy VM's, scoped-reload that one profile only (never a global teardown), then start and fully verify — including confirming the two unaffected VMs stayed healthy before and after. Zero AppArmor denials after the fix.

Lesson: "Failed to get write lock" from the hypervisor can be a file-open denial wearing a lock's mask. Trust the kernel audit log over the error string. And a VM that has gone through undefine / define can end up with stale security-policy artifacts that a normal re-define does not regenerate.

3. The IP migration, done right the second time. The first in-guest IP swap failed catastrophically (removed the management IP before the new one was confirmed — the session died and the auto-revert could not run, leaving the NIC with no address at all). The lesson: add the new IP alongside the old, verify reachability through a second session, then remove the old. The second attempt, using that dual-IP method, succeeded.

The stale-identity cleanup on the renamed DC — SPNs, DNS records, a stale DFSR topology object, and two false-success incidents where AD/DNS mutation cmdlets returned "OK" while changing nothing (wrong value types silently rejected; a DNS record not queryable as the AD object the cmdlet operated on). Details in §4.

The DemoteDC4 scheduled-task landmine — discovered incidentally, diagnosed, disabled, and removed, with all credential-bearing scripts scrubbed (see §4).

The identity saga proper — §5 below.

## 4. Troubleshooting index

Each entry: symptom → root cause → how it was diagnosed → fix.

4.1 adprep prompt hang (forestprep). Symptom: adprep /forestprep hung at 0% CPU with no output. Root cause: the tool's interactive "type C to continue" confirmation; over a remote session with no interactive stdin, the blocking read never returns. Diagnosis: process state (alive, idle, no output) + knowledge that the prompt exists; confirmed by the same hang class recurring elsewhere in the project (promotion prompts, FL-raise confirmations). Fix: pipe the answer into the process ( echo C | adprep.exe … ). Same family, same fix: promotion prompts, and (for the FL raise) the decision to run the command from a console instead (§3.7).

4.2 /gpPrep syntax error. Symptom: standalone /gpprep → RC=1, "Invalid syntax. /gpprep must be used with the /domainprep switch." Root cause: the switch is only valid combined with /domainprep . Fix: adprep.exe /domainprep /gpprep → RC=0. (Trivial in hindsight; recorded because it cost a cycle.)

4.3 Schema "anomaly" false alarm. Symptom: a pre-check reported a non-standard objectClass and an apparently abnormal schema state. Root cause: self-inflicted — the check queried a non-existent attribute and mis-read the schema NC head's class; objectClass = dMD on that head object is standard and expected . Diagnosis: re-queried with the authoritative method ( objectVersion on the schema NC head) → clean baseline (88), consistent with the 2016 functional level; class objects verified standard. Fix: none — no AD change was needed. Lesson: verify an "abnormal" AD reading with a second independent method before acting.

4.4 DSRM password policy wall + parameter changes on Server 2025. Symptom A: promotion rejected one DSRM candidate as "too short" and another as "too long" — both with the same generic error. Root cause A: the DSRM must satisfy the domain password policy , whose maximum length is hard-capped on this domain — so the double rejection was the diagnostic signature of a policy length cap, not two different failures. Fix A: use a DSRM that satisfies the domain policy. (Re-encountered again during the final rebuild: the below-policy candidate was rejected, the policy-compliant one accepted.) Symptom B: Install-ADDSDomainController on the 2025 build threw "parameter cannot be found" for parameters that exist in 2019-era docs. Root cause B: the 2025 cmdlet's parameter set changed. Fix B: probe the live parameter set ( Get-Command … -ParameterList ) and build the invocation from evidence. The asymmetry bites twice: Install-ADDSDomainController takes -SafeModeAdministratorPassword , while Uninstall-ADDSDomainController on 2025 takes -LocalAdministratorPassword and no longer has -SafeModeAdministratorPassword . Also: the Windows feature name for AD DS on 2025 is AD-Domain-Services (not the legacy name), and Install-WindowsFeature has no -NoReboot parameter on this build.

4.5 The DC4 identity saga. Told in full in §5. In one line: stale service-principal names for the box's old name kept reappearing within a minute of every clean removal, across three demote/re-promote cycles — until the record's decisive evidence (a reused, pre-existing damaged AD object) reframed the whole problem.

4.6 Hypervisor "write lock" failure that was actually AppArmor. Symptom: virsh start on one VM failed with "Failed to get write lock"; a libvirtd restart did not help. Root cause: AppArmor denial — the VM's per-domain profile included a .files fragment that did not exist on disk, and the domain XML under-listed the disk backing chain; the kernel audit log showed a plain read denied on the base disk file. Diagnosis: the misleading error string led first to a (wrong) orphaned-lock theory, formally withdrawn after lock-hunting found nothing. The ground truth was the kernel audit record: profile name, file, denied_mask="r" . Cross-referenced against a healthy VM's intact profile artifacts. Fix: rebuild the XML to the full backing chain; create the missing .files fragment mirroring the healthy VM's; scoped-reload only that one profile (no global teardown); start + verify; confirm the two unaffected VMs stayed healthy. Zero denials after. Lesson: trust the kernel audit log over the error text; undefine / define cycles can leave stale security-policy artifacts that a re-define does not regenerate.

4.7 The hypervisor snapshot-revert limitation (two encounters). Symptom: virsh snapshot-revert refused: "Invalid target domain state 'disk-snapshot'. Refusing." Root cause: the VM was in a disk-snapshot state that revert does not accept. Workaround: manual revert — destroy the VM, move the bad thin overlay aside (preserved for forensics), re-point the domain's system disk at the clean base image, re-define, start. Second encounter (later, worse): a "revert" to a snapshot had actually captured the post-mutation state — the snapshot had become the live disk (the snapshot-became-live-disk trap) — so the true pre-mutation image was the backing file. blockrevert / snapshot-revert were both unavailable; recovery was a backing-chain swap built with assertions against a self-referential chain (the first attempt failed with a lock error; the fixed builder asserted no self-reference before re-define). Lesson: before reverting, verify the snapshot's actual contents, not its name.

4.8 DNS forwarder and the 6900 loop. Symptom: during the identity saga, the identity-sync engine on member-sync-01 threw a storm of sync-failure event 6900s (~29 events in a 20-minute window), and AD-side lookups on the sync account looked disturbed. Working theory: the DCs' DNS forwarders had been lost, breaking external-name resolution needed by the sync engine. What the evidence actually showed: a same-day earlier read showed forwarders present on all three machines; a later read returned empty — an unresolved contradiction that was never re-verified . What did close: after the identity issues settled, no new 6900s appeared for 12+ hours and the engine cycled normally (its own healthy-cycle events present), so the 6900 storm was confirmed as a consequence of the identity/AD-side disturbance, not an independent DNS failure. The forwarder contradiction was left explicitly unresolved in the record. Honest status for publication: the 6900 loop is closed (no recurrence; engine healthy). The "forwarders lost" hypothesis is unverified — it was recorded as an open contradiction, never confirmed or refuted. Per the tasking, this is marked unverified rather than stated as fact.

4.9 The DemoteDC4 scheduled-task landmine. Symptom: an incidental read-only finding: a scheduled task on the renamed box, named for an old box, that ran a one-shot demotion script. Root cause (forensics): a leftover from an earlier automation attempt — created by the service account, running as SYSTEM, pointing at a script that invoked Uninstall-ADDSDomainController with a hardcoded plaintext credential . Its scheduled trigger window had already passed (last run: failed, result -1), but the task was still enabled and allowed on-demand firing — "Next Run Time: N/A" is not safety. Exposure: a manual/on-demand fire (or a future scheduler fix) would silently demote a live DC; the script also sat on the DC with embedded credentials. Remediation (authorized, staged): (1) disable the task (reversible) and verify state read-back; (2) unregister the task and delete all credential-bearing one-shot scripts from the DC, each verified gone; (3) confirm the DC still healthy afterward. Standing rules produced: a DC must never carry a task/script that can self-demote — especially in a small domain; Enabled=true + AllowStartOnDemand=true is armed even with a past-due schedule; never hardcode plaintext credentials in one-shot scripts on a DC.

4.10 The FL-raise WinRM lesson. Symptom (from earlier attempts): Set-ADForestMode / Set-ADDomainMode over the remote channel blocked on the interactive confirmation; each client timeout left an orphaned remote PowerShell on the DC holding an AD write lock ; the orphans stacked and eventually jammed even read-only AD queries. Root cause: long-running mutating AD writes over a stdin-less remote session with short client timeouts = orphan buildup + lock contention. Fix: run these writes from an interactive console ; the two FL raises then completed cleanly on the first try, with no orphans and no lock-jam. Verification: live read-back from both DC vantages. General rule: AD DS mutating writes that confirm interactively belong on a console; never trust the success line — the gate is always the read-back.

4.11 False-success incidents (two, both root-caused).

SPN removal "15 removed" that removed 0: the AD mutation call threw a type error (un-cast object array) but the session summary was written as success. The next day's re-check found all 15 stale SPNs still present. Fix: cast the value array properly; rule: the action token ( OK / ERR ) is the only ground truth, never the prose summary — and always reconcile with an independent post-state count.

DNS delete "DELETE-OK" that deleted nothing: the record lived in the DNS zone store but was not exposed as the AD object the AD cmdlet operated on, so the cmdlet matched nothing and "succeeded" benignly while the record kept resolving. Fix: use the DNS management module's record-delete path (the legacy CLI path was refused by the zone's security ACL); rule: a cmdlet returning success over an ambiguous identity is not proof of the intended mutation — read the record back first.

4.12 Other cataloged items (for completeness). virsh reboot is a no-op on these guests (verify reboots by uptime/last-boot time, never domstate ); msiexec /x hung on the sync agent's packages four times (switch to direct removal once a "standard" tool keeps wedging); QEMU VNC is single-client (a stray client black-screens noVNC — kill the stale one); repadmin "110/1" lines are query-timeout noise, not replication failures; a rollback script's sed pattern silently no-oped against the hypervisor's XML tag format (caught by an end-state assertion; fixed with a first-occurrence-only replace plus post-write verification).

## 5. The DC4 saga, told properly

The symptom, in one sentence. After the renamed box took on the original identity, its AD object kept re-accumulating the old name's service-principal names — 15 stale SPNs reappearing within 60 seconds of every clean, verified removal, across three separate demote/re-promote cycles, plus a stale DNS record and a stale DFSR topology object. The domain was, at points, effectively running on a single DC, or on one healthy DC plus a zombie whose AD-side identity had been deleted.

Why this section is honest about the timeline: the wrong theories were pursued across multiple sessions, before the actual root cause was read out of the directory itself. The sequence below is the order the theories were actually tried and ruled out.

Registry hostname (the "identity writer"). The first identity crisis was fixed by finding stale Tcpip\Parameters hostname keys feeding DNS self-registration — every registration re-painted the old FQDN and re-added the factory SPNs. That fix worked at the time . In the later crises, the same key was fixed again, the LSA cache was rebuilt after reboot, the SPNs were cleanly removed — and the exact same 15 re-appeared within 60 seconds . Ruled out: while the registry key was a real identity source, it was not the writer of the recurring pattern.

LSA cache / CachedMachineNames . Deleted and rebuilt (the stale old-name entry was present, fixed, verified). The re-addition continued. Ruled out.

Netlogon in-memory state. Service restarted, then a full reboot (fresh state, twice). The re-addition continued. Ruled out.

Replication conflict / stale-replica model. Two checks killed it: no conflict events (the 2087–2091 family) anywhere, and the decisive observation — after a clean delete on the PDC, the PDC stayed clean for the full 180-second watch while the other DC went dirty locally . A stale replica that was "newer" would have won the merge and pushed the SPNs back to the PDC ; it did the opposite. The writer was a live process acting locally on the box — but not via replication, and not via any of the local state above. Ruled out.

AD Connect (identity-sync) writeback. The sync service's accounts held inherited write grants on computer objects, the inclusion scope covered computer objects, and 4662 read events (not 5136 writes — auditing was never enableable over the available channel) showed a ~2-minute cadence matching the re-add windows. It was the strongest remaining writer candidate and stayed under operator HOLD (logs-only, no rule changes). It was never positively proven — and it didn't need to be, because the next piece of evidence reframed everything.

Wrong-DN removal bug. An earlier "removal succeeded" report was actually failing with "Directory object not found" because the DN used the non-existent CN=Computers container instead of OU=Domain Controllers . Fixed and proven (15/15 clean removal) — and the SPNs still came back. Ruled out as the persistent cause.

The actual root cause — found by reading the directory's own metadata, not by hunting processes:

CN=DC-B,OU=Domain Controllers : created well before the final promotion — with a fixed object GUID, low historical USN.

Its DSA object ( NTDS Settings ) was freshly created at the final promotion.

Conclusion: Install-ADDSDomainController was reusing the pre-existing, damaged computer object — the scar tissue of every prior crisis lived on the AD object itself — and attaching a brand-new DSA to it. The box's local copy of that object carried the old SPN list at promotion time and held the higher USN, so it re-asserted the stale SPNs and won every DRS merge against scrubs performed from the other DC (lower USN can never win). This single fact explains why a "fresh install" reproduced the identical symptom across three demote/re-promote cycles, and why no local-state cleanup could ever stick.

A fourth orphan object made it worse than the two-object case implied: a stray computer object in the wrong container sharing the same machine-account name as the DC object — a hard identity conflict, leftover from the very first broken join attempt (the join that reported OK but left the box in WORKGROUP).

The fix, in three verified steps: (1) demote (the 2025 parameter set, again); (2) delete the entire object family — the DC object, its DSA, the stale DFSR topology member, and the fourth orphan — each verified GONE from the authoritative DC's view, with a domain-wide sweep confirming zero stale-name SPNs remained; (3) rebuild the VM from scratch and re-promote against the now-empty name — which forced the promotion to mint a brand-new AD object. Acceptance check that proves it was genuinely new: whenCreated = today, and a different object GUID than the old one. The post-promotion stability watch (multiple samples, both vantages) held clean: zero stale SPNs, stable count, replication 0/5 both directions, FSMO intact on the primary, global catalog active. The saga closed cleanly.

What this costs in hindsight: at least three full demote/re-promote cycles, two single-DC exposure windows, one zombie DC, one credential lockout, and a long stretch of the project's remaining calendar — all because the fix had to start from "which AD object is this box actually running on?" instead of "which process is writing?" The single most valuable move in the whole saga was the day someone stopped diagnosing the box and started reading the object's creation date and GUID .

## 6. What I'd do differently

Never rename a DC in place. It is the single most expensive decision in this project. In-place identity changes on a DC leave writers in places you can't enumerate — registry identity sources, LSA cache, keytabs, service SPNs, DFSR topology, DNS stores — and the DC4 saga shows a long stretch of effort spent proving each of them wasn't the cause.

Build with the final names from the start. If the end goal is "the primary DC is called the original name at the original IP," build the new primary as that name from the start (the old box's machine account can be deleted once demoted, which frees the name for a clean netdom /ADD or even a fresh build). The swing migration is the same work; the rename phase is pure risk.

Check whether a promotion reuses an existing AD object — before and after every Install-ADDSDomainController . Two read-only checks cost nothing and would have saved the project considerable effort: read whenCreated and objectGUID of the resulting OU=Domain Controllers object after promotion. A whenCreated older than the promotion means a damaged object was reused and the box must be demoted, its object family deleted, and re-promoted.

Check DNS (servers, zones, forwarders) early — and re-verify after every identity change. The 6900 loop, the stale-record cleanup, and the forwarder contradiction were all downstream of name/DNS churn. DNS state should be a first-class read-back gate on every mutation, not an afterthought.

Make independent read-back mandatory after every mutation — no exceptions. Two "verified" successes in this project were both wrong (SPN removal that never ran; DNS delete that matched nothing). The pattern that caught both: a second, independent read of the intended final state, on the authoritative vantage, time-gapped. The action token is truth; the prose summary is not.

Search the project's own past successful fixes before building a new theory tree. The registry-identity-writer fix from the first crisis was the key to reframing the saga; it had to be re-discovered by re-reading an old session log during the crisis.

Keep a DC clean of self-demotion artifacts. The DemoteDC4 task (armed, enabled, hardcoded credential, past-due schedule) was a live gun in the domain. Standing rule: no Uninstall-ADDSDomainController -capable task or script may exist on a DC; check Enabled / AllowStartOnDemand , not just "Next Run Time."

Treat "Failed to get write lock" from the hypervisor as unproven. Read the kernel audit log first — in this project it was an AppArmor file-open denial, and the wrong lock theory consumed a full session.

## 7. Final state and what's still open

## 7.1 Verified final state (closeout)

Item
State

Domain contoso.example , 2 live DCs

DC A (primary) Windows Server 2025, 192.0.2.4, all 5 FSMO roles , global catalog, replication 0-fail both vantages

DC B Windows Server 2025, 192.0.2.2 (original primary identity), global catalog, fresh AD object (new GUID, today's creation date), 0 stale SPNs, autostart enabled

Identity sync member-sync-01 @ 192.0.2.6, engine live and healthy, timezone aligned to the DCs

Functional level Windows 2025 forest + domain (irreversible step complete, both vantages verified)

Old 2019 DCs dc-01 and dc-02 demoted, powered off, retained (disk images + all snapshots as rollback material)

Hypervisor snapshots 34+ retained per policy (baseline, pre-forestprep, pre-domainprep, pre-join, pre-promo, pre-demote, pre-flraise, pre-rename, pre-ipchange, pre-demote-rebuild, and others)

Lab note This was a lab/POC environment — single hypervisor host, evaluation OS editions, single-domain forest. Findings on cmdlet parameter changes, AD-object reuse, AppArmor/libvirt interaction, and the discipline itself transfer directly to production forests; the credential-handling notes deliberately do not.

## 7.2 Still open (all optional; none block dual-DC health)

dc-03 rename (→ the original secondary identity). Parked by operator decision: if it is ever wanted, it will be done as a fresh build, never in place , and will be requested separately.

The retained zombie VM (the old DC4 disk image, shut off, autostart disabled, restorable). Decommission or repurpose is a separate decision; it is not required for dual-DC health.

The member-sync-01 event log shows repeated GroupPolicy 1125 errors — flagged for investigation; the sync engine itself is healthy (live, cycling normally), so this is cosmetic-or-unknown, not confirmed harmful. (Unverified in the record — marked as such.)

Snapshot pruning. 34+ snapshots are retained by policy; cleanup requires an explicit operator decision.

The DNS-forwarder contradiction (empty vs. populated forwarder reads on the same day) was never re-verified; if forwarders were genuinely lost, the 6900 symptom class could return. Re-check Get-DnsServerForwarders on both DCs before dismissing. (Unverified in the record — marked as such.)

Stale DHCP static reservation on the lab network for the retired primary DC's MAC — dormant collision risk if that VM ever boots and DHCPs; low urgency while it stays off.

## 8. Appendix — the discipline that made this survivable

For a reader with no project context, the pattern worth copying is not any single fix but the operating loop that repeated ~40 times in this project:

snapshot → GO → execute → independent read-back (authoritative vantage)
→ time-gapped re-read → report (including what still fails)

Snapshot before every mutation — 34+ rollback points, several of which were used.

Independent read-back — from the other DC's vantage, not the box that just changed; time-gapped where identity was in question (the 60-second SPN watch is what proved a live writer existed).

Report the failures — the two false successes (§4.11) were caught precisely because the next session's first act was re-verification, not trust.

Stop-and-report gates — the single-DC exposure windows stayed windows , not outages, because every destructive step waited for explicit authorization and every recovery was offered as options, not executed.

Evidence over error strings — the AppArmor case, the realm-mismatch case, and the reused-object case were all solved by reading ground truth (kernel audit log, AD object metadata, KDC behavior) instead of trusting the surface error.

Prepared from the full project record ( DCupgrade-STATE.md , MIGRATION-LOG.md , and the working case-study entries). No state-changing commands were run to produce this document. Retracted claims from earlier in the project — the "orphaned flock" theory, the AD Connect writeback theory, "dual-DC restored" statements that later proved to describe a zombie, and the "15 SPNs removed" reports that removed zero — are not carried forward as fact; they appear above only as the diagnosed dead ends they were.
