summary: How a disciplined audit — evidence first, fix second, verify third — found and closed the real security gaps behind a working Azure domain…
text:
Auditing and Securing a Domain Controller on Azure | AppoSight



## Auditing and Securing a Domain Controller on Azure

How a disciplined audit — evidence first, fix second, verify third — found and closed the real security gaps behind a working Azure domain controller: weak IPsec crypto, a 16,384-port firewall grant, a VPN CA key sitting on a workstation, and privileged accounts out of scope. An AI agent did the hunting and the proving; a human approved every privileged change — and the most sensitive one stays in human hands to apply.

Companion to the "Deploying a Domain Controller to Azure" case study. That project built the Azure DC and proved it replicates. This one secures it.

## The starting problem

The first case study ended with a working, replicating domain controller in Azure. But "working" is not "secure." The tunnel that makes the Azure DC useful is also its only front door, and a quick look at the live state showed four gaps that a customer or a regulator would immediately notice:

# Gap (as found) Severity
W1 The IPsec tunnel was negotiating AES-128-CBC / SHA-1 / MODP-1024 — an audit-visible weak combination, in a tunnel that is the only path to a domain controller High
W2 The NSG allowed 16,384 inbound RPC/DFSR/DNS ports to the DC (range 49152–65535) Medium
W3 The point-to-site VPN root-CA private key — and the client certificate — sat as plaintext files on a workstation: a single point of failure for the entire VPN identity Medium
W4 The Windows baseline of the DC itself had never been audited: privileged groups, local accounts, RDP group, services Medium

The working rule for this whole track was the same as the build: evidence before assertion, a state change only after an explicit human approval, and secrets handled as references — never values.

## The method

Every finding followed the same loop: capture the live state as evidence → propose the smallest change that closes the gap → apply only after approval → verify the after-state with the same tool that produced the before-state. Where a tool could not see in (a service-account context, a locked file, a kernel counter), the gap was recorded as inconclusive — never quietly read as "compliant."

## What the audit found

## W1 — The tunnel was quietly negotiating weak crypto

The tunnel reported healthy, connected, and moving data on both ends. But its own status output showed the negotiated proposal: AES_CBC_128 / HMAC_SHA1 / MODP_1024 . The cause was subtle: the gateway had no explicit IPsec policy, so it had fallen back to a default set that included the weak pair. No error, no warning — just a weak handshake in a log nobody was reading.

The fix was a two-sided pin, chosen to the strongest combination the gateway class actually supports (the DH-group ceiling was checked against the live --help , not assumed): AES-256 / SHA-384 / ECP-384 in the IKE phase and AES-256-GCM in the ESP phase on both Azure and strongSwan.

This is where the verification discipline paid off, in the form of a mistake the agent itself made and caught. The first rekey dropped the tunnel: the IKE phase was pinned correctly but the ESP line was missing its ECP group, so on the first rekey Azure offered GCM over ECP-384 while the local side offered GCM over MODP-2048 — no common proposal, and the tunnel silently died. The signature looked exactly like a network outage. It was root-caused to that one token, corrected to …-ecp384 , and re-keyed. The lesson recorded: an "IKE up, ESP dead" state is indistinguishable from a tunnel outage unless you read both phases — and a rekey failure is not proof the fix was wrong, only proof something is still mismatched.

## W2 — A 16,384-port grant, narrowed to the ports that were actually listening

The NSG rule was 49152–65535 — a blanket 16,384-port allow to a domain controller. The audit did not guess at a "safe range"; it read the actual live listeners on the box and found the real set was far smaller: RPC endpoint mapper on 135, the LSASS LDAP endpoints in 49664–49704, ADWS, and the two service ports for DFSR and DNS.

The change was the smallest one that closed the gap with zero Windows-state impact: narrow the NSG to exactly the observed listener set. No service restart, no LDAP rebind, fully reversible with a single command.

Before → after: 16,384 allowed inbound RPC/DFSR/DNS ports → 43 (41 in 49664–49704, plus DFSR and DNS), all still scoped to the single trusted source.

Verified by a port matrix, not a claim: in-range ports (389, 135, 49664, 53281, 56715) open, and previously-allowed out-of-range ports (49153, 50000, 60000) now filtered — the hardening is visible, not assumed. AD replication, the function that actually depends on those ports, stayed green through and after the change.

## W3 — A VPN CA key living on a workstation

The gateway held only the root certificate ; the private key was needed only to sign a new client certificate. But that key — plus the client key and certificate — was sitting as plaintext files on a workstation. A single lost or stolen workstation was a total compromise of the VPN identity.

The fix moved all four files into a local, encrypted vault (gpg, AES-256, PBKDF2), with a passphrase generated and shown to the human exactly once and never recorded. Every file was round-trip verified (decrypt, hash-match, size-match), then the plaintext originals — including a stray duplicate — were shredded and a full-disk sweep confirmed no P2S private key remained anywhere on the host.

Verified: the decrypted root key's public half matches the certificate already installed on the gateway — so the vault holds the correct key, not a copy of something else.

## W4 — The DC's own Windows baseline

This is the audit that found the most, because it was the least looked at. A read-only sweep of the live DC surfaced:

High: the Guest account enabled; the Print Spooler running and set to auto-start on a domain controller (a PrintNightmare-class surface that has no business there); and three human-named local SAM accounts enabled that shadow real users — a pass-the-hash / local-privilege path.

Medium: ~36 local SAM accounts created locally on the DC rather than as domain accounts; a privileged service account holding the two highest-privilege groups plus operator groups; a recurring Group Policy failure the logs flagged but the service-account context could not fully explain.

The agent remediated the High items it could reach in-context and verified each with the same command that produced the finding:

H1 Guest account -> disabled (verified: Enabled=False)
H2 Print Spooler -> Stopped, Disabled (verified: State/StartType)
H3 3 human-named local SAM -> disabled (verified: Enabled=False each)

During remediation, a transient state reading briefly suggested the three accounts might have re-enabled themselves — a discrepancy serious enough to warrant a full stop and independent investigation before proceeding further. A dedicated audit-log review found zero account-enable events across the entire window, from any source, and traced the only account-modification activity to the remediation script's own service context. A second, independent re-verification twenty-four hours later — fresh event log query, fresh account-state read — confirmed the same result: all three accounts remain disabled, and no enable event exists anywhere in the log. The original reading is best explained as a transient capture artifact, not a real state change or unauthorized action. The finding: closed, with two independent confirmations rather than one.

The Medium item of a privileged service account with excess rights was identified, scoped for reduction, and staged and handed to the operator to apply over an interactive RDP session — the kind of change to a production AD identity that the operating model deliberately keeps in human hands (see below). A few lines — Group Policy root cause, Defender signature currency, SMB signing, TLS minimum version — sit behind an elevated interactive session the audit context could not read; they are reported as inconclusive , not "compliant."

## The durability test

A security fix that vanishes on reboot is not a fix. The on-prem host is on a nightly power schedule, so the real test was whether the whole secured stack — tunnel, firewall order, replication — came back up on its own after a full power cycle, unattended.

It did, and it had already survived one: a prior reboot had regenerated one of the firewall chains empty, breaking one direction of AD replication with a single, direction-specific error. The agent's recovery script was rewritten to verify the rule's position and correctness , not just its presence, so the next reboot did not reproduce the failure. On the following power cycle, the tunnel auto-reconnected within seconds, the firewall rules were re-pinned at the correct chain positions, and AD replication was green in both directions across all three domain controllers with no manual intervention.

## Where the human stayed in control

The build case study's rule held, and got stricter, because this track is privilege-reducing rather than build-out:

Every privileged state change was human-approved before it ran — and the most sensitive one was never run by the agent. The de-scoping of a production AD service account was identified, scoped, and staged by the agent, then handed to the operator to apply over RDP, so the AD-identity change stays in human hands.

Credentials and secrets stayed out of the agent's reach. The CA vault passphrase was generated and shown once, then discarded from the tooling; the DC's privileged-account de-scope was staged by the agent and reserved for the operator to apply over RDP.

A state discrepancy was treated as a stop-and-verify event, not a footnote. When remediation evidence briefly disagreed with itself, the response was to halt, pull the authoritative audit log, and re-confirm independently — twice — rather than resolve it by assertion.

Findings the tools could not prove were labeled as such. Inconclusive was kept inconclusive — a "can't see it" was never written up as a "pass."

## Verified outcome

The decisive check — the same command the build used, re-run after the audit — is unchanged and green. Verbatim from the audit window ( ops/w4-D-out.txt ):

repadmin /replsummary

Source DSA largest delta fails/total %% error
CONTO-DC 12m:56s 0 / 10 0
CONTO-DC2 12m:56s 0 / 10 0
vm-w2022-poc 02m:38s 0 / 10 0

Destination DSA largest delta fails/total %% error
CONTO-DC 02m:39s 0 / 10 0
CONTO-DC2 :51s 0 / 10 0
vm-w2022-poc 12m:58s 0 / 10 0

Zero replication failures, in both directions, across all three domain controllers. The same check was re-run live after the subsequent power cycle and security changes, and returned the same result — zero failures in both directions. The tunnel was on the hardened AES-256/GCM/ECP-384 policy, the NSG narrowed to the observed listener set, the VPN CA key off-host, and the DC's High-severity local-account and service findings closed.

## What this actually demonstrates

The build proved an AI agent can do hard systems work end-to-end. The audit adds the part that's more valuable in practice: the agent can find the gaps a working system hides, and — more importantly — prove which of its own fixes are real. It caught its own crypto pinning mistake from the rekey failure, distinguished a "tunnel down" from an "ESP mismatch," treated a self-contradicting piece of evidence as a reason to stop and dig deeper rather than explain away, refused to read a tool it couldn't see through as "compliant," and left every AD-identity decision to the human.

That boundary — evidence before assertion, approval before privilege, and "inconclusive" left honestly inconclusive — is the part of the model that a customer can actually rely on.

Building a Secure AKS Employee Portal Backend on Azure with an AI Agent | AppoSight



## Building a Secure AKS Employee Portal Backend on Azure with an AI Agent

How an AI agent provisioned a no-secrets, fully identity-based AKS + SQL + Key Vault + ACR stack for an employee portal — then validated, revoked, and tore it all down cleanly, with a human approving every privileged step.

## 1. Objective & scope

What was built. A small, cost-conscious AKS cluster in Azure that hosts an internal employee portal. The deployment doubles as a teaching case study — the bar is clear, well-documented, standard patterns over clever configuration , and every design choice is explainable to a learner.

Why. The project exercises three PSC lines simultaneously:

D-IT — cloud infrastructure / platform engineering (AKS, VNet, NSG, ACR, Key Vault, SQL, Log Analytics).

R-mgmt — the audit-then-deploy, cost-cap, evidence-first discipline that governed the whole engagement.

U-training — the case-study narrative itself is the deliverable.

Locked scope (do not re-open without explicit approval).

Employee-portal only. Internal, no public exposure. No customer / B2C path.

No VPN gateway. The portal is reached over the VNet / internal LB. A live site-to-site tunnel is not required to demonstrate any of the PoC's actual goals.

Infrastructure + identity plumbing only. End-to-end application login was intentionally not exercised — the ILB backend pool is empty by design , and the portal application layer is out of scope for this PoC . This is a scope boundary, not an oversight (see §6).

Budget cap: $300 / month with alerts at 50 / 80 / 100 % to the budget-alert recipient.

What was removed from the original two-portal brief (public customer + internal employee) when the scope was narrowed to employee-only:

App Gateway v2 + OWASP WAF

Public IP (for inbound)

Public-ingress subnet

Public NSG

Any B2C / public-identity path

## 3. Design decisions & tradeoffs

Each major fork in the road, the decision, and the reason.

## 3.1 Two-portal → employee-only scope narrowing

Decision. Narrow the original two-portal brief (public customer + internal employee) to employee-only .

Why. The PoC's actual goals — AKS, RBAC, Key Vault, ACR, SQL, Azure AD auth — are all internal. A customer-facing path (App Gateway v2 + OWASP WAF, public IP, public-ingress subnet, public NSG, B2C) was not required to demonstrate any of them, and it was the largest source of cost and complexity. Removing it:

Cut the largest cost line (~$142 / mo for the gateway, §3.3)

Removed the recurring East US SKU failure source

Left the design strictly internal (no public IP at all — a strict improvement over the gateway design)

What changed in the templates. App Gateway v2 + OWASP WAF, public IP, public-ingress subnet, public NSG, and any B2C / public-identity path removed from main.bicep / cluster.bicep .

## 3.2 Entra External ID considered and ruled out

Decision. Not used. No customer population means no External ID requirement.

Why. The portal is employee-only; the existing <organization-domain> Entra tenant already provides the OIDC issuer and the RBAC model ( aadProfile managed=true , enableAzureRBAC=true ). Adding External ID / B2C would have introduced a second identity platform, a separate tenant boundary, and a separate set of RBAC grants — none of which the PoC needs.

Note for future readers: Azure AD B2C is closed to new customers as of May 2025. Entra External ID (the successor) is the supported path going forward. If a future PoC does need a customer / B2C path, budget for External ID onboarding, not B2C.

## 3.3 VPN Gateway dropped from PoC scope

Decision (b, 2026-08-25). Drop the VPN Gateway. No Central US gateway test, no East US quota support ticket.

Why.

The employee portal is already internal / VNet-reached via the Internal LB ; none of the PoC's goals (AKS, RBAC, Key Vault, ACR, SQL, Azure AD auth) require a live site-to-site tunnel.

The gateway was the largest cost line (~$142 / mo) and the repeated source of East US InvalidGatewaySkuSpecified failures on VpnGw1 / VpnGw2 Standard (see §4.2).

The design therefore has no public IP at all (pure internal path) — a strict improvement over the gateway design.

Temporary admin/office access during the PoC window is provided by the scoped allow-office NSG rule ( <office-source-cidr> → 80/443), not a VPN. That rule is PoC-only — not a production access pattern — and is removed with the rest of the PoC at teardown.

What changed in the templates. gw-basic.bicep / gw-test.bicep / gw-v2.bicep (+ compiled .json ) are out of the active deploy path (not referenced by main.bicep / cluster.bicep ); kept in the repo only as historical test-harness evidence. GatewaySubnet resource, gatewaySubnetCidr / gatewayLocation / vpnSku params, and the gateway + gateway public-IP resources removed. vpnSourceCidr param renamed officeSourceCidr ( <office-source-cidr> ) — it now feeds the allow-office NSG rule.

## 3.4 Cosmos DB considered and ruled out in favor of Azure SQL Database Serverless

Decision. Use Azure SQL Database Serverless v1 (centralus, single database employeedb , schemas for the portal's relational data), not Cosmos DB.

Why.

Relational data model. The portal's data is inherently relational (employees, departments, access records). Cosmos DB's document model would have forced a denormalized design and a different query language for data that is naturally tabular.

Simpler cost model. SQL Serverless with minCapacity=1 vCore + autoPauseDelay=3600 s bounds the cost to ~$20–150 / mo and auto-pauses when idle. Cosmos DB's RU-based pricing is harder to reason about for a PoC and has a different floor.

Simpler identity. One SQL Server Contributor role on the shared MI is straightforward. Cosmos DB would have required a separate RBAC model (Cosmos DB Account Reader / Data Contributor) and a different set of connection-string mechanics.

## 3.5 Bicep two-file split (subscription-scope entrypoint + resourceGroup-scope module)

Decision. Split the template into main.bicep (subscription scope) + cluster.bicep (resourceGroup scope), with an explicit scope: rg on the module reference.

Why. Bicep cannot mix subscription-scoped resources (the Resource Group) and resourceGroup-scoped resources (AKS, VNet, …) in one file — it emits BCP135 . And this Bicep build requires an explicit scope on a module that crosses from a subscription-scoped file into a resourceGroup-scoped target — BCP035 / BCP134 . The two-file split is the only clean way to satisfy both constraints.

## 4. What went wrong, and how it was resolved

This is the most valuable section for a teaching case study. Do not sanitize it.

## 4.1 Parallel subnet writes → AnotherOperationInProgress / Conflict (5 failed deploys)

Symptom. After the gateway was dropped, deploys failed with AnotherOperationInProgress / Conflict on Microsoft.Network — and the failing subnet changed each run ( aks-node , then internal-ingress , then aks-node again).

Root cause. Three subnets of one VNet were being created concurrently , which Azure's Network service rejects non-deterministically.

Fix. Serialize subnet creation with a dependsOn chain: vnet → nodeSubnet → internalSubnet → systemSubnet , with AKS and Key Vault created after the subnets. Also fixed: the agent pool vnetSubnetID originally pointed at the system subnet while the KV ACL + SQL firewall are scoped to aks-node — re-pointed at nodeSubnet so pods can actually reach KV / SQL.

Lesson. Provision subnets serially or with explicit dependsOn from the start. Do not rely on Bicep's implicit dependency ordering for resources that the underlying service rejects in parallel.

## 4.2 East US VPN Gateway / SQL SKU-availability restrictions

Symptom. Two separate East US restrictions on this subscription:

VPN Gateway: InvalidGatewaySkuSpecified on VpnGw1 / VpnGw2 Standard in East US.

SQL Server: "Provisioning is restricted in this region" for new SQL servers in East US.

Resolution.

Gateway: dropped from scope entirely (decision b, §3.3). No longer a blocker.

SQL: relocated to centralus (approved by user, "2 a"). Consequence: publicNetworkAccess must be Enabled (VNet service endpoints are same-region only) — documented as a PoC-only tradeoff; tighten the firewall before any production use.

Lesson. Check regional SKU availability before designing around a specific gateway or SQL SKU. Query az aks get-versions / az sql servers list-skus / az network vpn-gateway list-skus for the target region and subscription before committing a design.

Symptom. Microsoft.Resources/budgets returns 404 at both subscription and tenant scope for this tenant (provider is Registered, but the resourceType is not exposed — verified at sub AND tenant scope, api-versions 2024-03-01 / 2022-09-01).

## 4.4 AKS version / VM-size SKU restrictions in East US

Symptom. Two East US restrictions on this subscription:

K8sVersionNotSupported : 1.31.3 is now LTS-only in East US (only 1.31.13 / 1.31.100 LTS patches are GA).

VM size not allowed : Standard_D2s_v5 is not in the allowed-VM-sizes list for this subscription in East US.

## 4.5 Container Insights DCR / DCRA binding failure (AAD → API-server propagation lag)

Symptom. Container Insights is not bound to the Log Analytics workspace. All control-plane indicators confirm this:

addonProfiles: null on the cluster

Zero DCRs and zero DCRA associations

The workspace cpcs-log exists (PerGB2018) but has no data

A separate finding, surfaced while trying to verify the cluster from inside: a temporary AAD cluster-admin grant was registered on the cluster ( aadProfile.adminGroupObjectIDs updated, HTTP 200) for the <deployment-service-principal> SP (object ID <deployment-service-principal-object-id> ). Despite ~15 minutes of wait + repeated fresh-token attempts, the API server kept rejecting: User "<deployment-service-principal-object-id>" cannot list resource "services" … User does not have access to the resource in Azure — an AAD → API-server propagation / staleness issue outside our control. Resolution (approval 2, 2026-08-26). Accepted as a documented limitation — no further fix attempts (no Portal path, no further DCR / DCRA iterations). The evidence-backed record of this gap is itself a real, evidence-backed finding. No further action is required on this item before publishing.

Lesson. AAD RBAC grants on AKS can lag the API server by 15+ minutes even after the aadProfile is updated and a fresh token is minted. And the API can return HTTP 200 on a PATCH that does nothing — always re-read the field you tried to set.

## 4.6 Post-outage AD replication anomaly (DC1 frozen, DC2 green)

Context. A separate, on-prem AD / DC environment (DC1 = DC1 <dc-internal-ip> , DC2 = DC2 <dc-internal-ip> , both Windows Server 2019, libvirt VMs on a homelab host) suffered a power outage on 2026-08-26. After the host rebooted (06:43 CDT), DC1's inbound-from-DC2 replication state was frozen at the outage window while DC2's own view was green. DC2 was restored from KVM (autostart enabled on both VMs), and the dead PoC neighbor ( <poc-vm> , an Azure-DC PoC VM that had been torn down the previous night) was still emitting error 1722 (RPC server unavailable) on 32 consecutive syncs on DC1 and 11 on DC2.

Decision path.

Passive vs. forced sync. Chose passive first : let the KDC / LDAP services settle, verify all 7 AD ports (389 / 88 / 53 / 445 / 135 / 3268 / 5985) open on both DCs, then run a scoped, bounded repadmin /syncall DC1 /A (DC2-only-inbound variant) with a 15-minute hard cap. Did not do a forced /replsync or any authoritative state change.

Orphaned repadmin processes. A prior full /syncall had hung for 73+ minutes on DC1, leaving 2 orphaned repadmin.exe processes (PID 1184, PID 4360) blocked on LDAP timeouts to the dead neighbor. Decision: kill only those two PIDs (client-side sync helpers — not lsass.exe or ntds ), confirm no other repadmin is running, and do not open a second WinRM connection mid-sync. When the targeted kill script ran, the orphans had already self-terminated (their LDAP timeout cycles expired) — the guard correctly found count 0 and did not execute taskkill . Zero repadmin processes confirmed.

Scoped sync result. SCOPED_RUN_EXIT=0 , completed in ~90 s (well under the cap). Before / after (raw, both DCs):
Before (pre-sync, 07:50): DC1 → DC2 5/5 fails (1722) on DomainDnsZones / ForestDnsZones; DC1 inbound-neighbor <poc-vm> 32 consecutive fails.

After (post-sync, 17:11): DC1 → DC2 0/5 fails, delta < 30 m , all 5 partitions Last attempt was successful ; DC2 → DC1 0/5 fails . replsummary: DC2 42m:31s 0/5 0 ; DC1 49m:35s 0/5 0 .

The 58 - <poc-vm> line in replsummary's "operational errors" section remained until the dead-neighbor metadata was removed (§8.2).

Final clean resolution. The dead PoC neighbor was fully removed (connection objects + DSA tree + DNS + computer / server / DFSR metadata — see §8.2), and after that removal the error 58 line disappeared and the forest-wide replsummary was clean. No metadata cleanup, USN rollback, or authoritative state change was ever required or performed — the scoped sync + targeted dead-neighbor removal resolved everything cleanly.

Lesson. A frozen replication state on one DC while the other is green is usually a client-side / transport problem (orphaned sync helpers, a dead neighbor, or a post-reboot service not yet listening), not a directory corruption. Do not reach for USN rollback or authoritative restore first — verify the services, clear the orphans, run a bounded scoped sync, and only escalate to metadata surgery if the scoped sync still shows failures on a live neighbor.

## 5.3 No-secrets-in-code discipline

Principle. Secrets live in Key Vault, wired via Managed Identity. No client secrets, no K8s-native secret objects, no admin keys.

Key Vault: <kv-name> (standard, soft-delete 90 d, purge protection ON, network ACL scoped to the two subnets). Pods access via Key Vault CSI driver + the shared MI — no client secrets, no K8s-native secret objects.

ACR: adminUserEnabled=false , anonymousPullEnabled=false . AKS pulls via the shared MI (AcrPull role). No admin keys ever issued.

SQL: admin password is a file on the operator's workstation ( <sql-admin-password-file> , mode 600) — never in the Bicep, never in the repo, never in the write-up. The Bicep takes it as a param and passes it to the administratorLoginPassword field; the value is supplied at deploy time from the secure file.

SSH key: public key only, wired into cluster.bicep as ssh.publicKeys[0].keyData . The private key is stored securely outside version control (operator workstation).

SP credentials: <deployment-service-principal> creds live in a secure file on the operator's workstation (referenced by path only, never by value).

Lesson. The test of a no-secrets design is not "is there a Key Vault?" — it is "does the Bicep, the repo, the logs, or the write-up contain a secret value?" This PoC passes that test: the Bicep contains only references to secrets, not values.

❌ AuthorizationFailed — ABAC condition on the assignment itself: holder may not write / delete UAM, User Access Administrator, or Owner ( GuidNotEquals {<role-def-uam-condition-1>, <role-def-uam-condition-2>, <role-def-uam-condition-3>} on both write and delete ). This is the by-design UAM self-protection condition.

Post-revocation live role assignment list

Manual step ( <org-owner> — performed by the human Owner, not by <deployment-service-principal> itself):

az role assignment delete \
--assignee <deployment-service-principal-object-id> \
--role "User Access Administrator" \
--scope /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>

Run as any subscription Owner / Administrator (e.g. the Microsoft account behind <org-admin-email> ), then re-run az role assignment list --assignee <deployment-service-principal-object-id> to confirm zero rows. Rationale it's safe: the SP has no remaining resource-group scope after teardown; the only live entitlement is this one subscription-level assignment. (Alternatively disable the SP: az ad sp update --id <deployment-service-principal-client-id> --set disabled=true — immediate, reversible.)

Status (verified 2026-08-27): the UAM assignment has been deleted and independently re-verified — a fresh az role assignment list for this SP (subscription scope) returns empty , so <deployment-service-principal> holds zero standing role assignments. This closes the last item from the AKS PoC teardown. No open items remain from the AKS PoC teardown.

## 8.2 Post-outage cleanup (the AD / DC environment, 2026-08-26)

This is a separate environment (on-prem AD / DC, not the AKS PoC), but it is part of the same engagement's cleanup scope. The power outage on 2026-08-26 left the following residue:

8.2.1 Dead PoC neighbor removal ( <poc-vm> )

The Azure-DC PoC VM ( <poc-vm> , <poc-vm-ip> ) had been torn down the previous night, but its AD metadata (connection objects, DSA tree, DNS records, computer / server / DFSR objects) was still present on both DCs and was the source of the error 1722 / error 58 replication failures.

## 9. Lessons for future PoCs

Provision subnets serially or with explicit dependsOn from the start. Azure's Network service rejects concurrent writes to subnets of the same VNet with AnotherOperationInProgress / Conflict . Do not rely on Bicep's implicit dependency ordering for resources that the underlying service rejects in parallel. (§4.1)

Check regional SKU availability before designing around a specific gateway or SQL SKU. Query az aks get-versions / az sql servers list-skus / az network vpn-gateway list-skus for the target region and subscription before committing a design. East US rejected both the VPN Gateway (VpnGw1 / VpnGw2 Standard) and new SQL provisioning for this subscription. (§4.2, §4.4)

Verify Microsoft.Resources/budgets is exposed in the target tenant before relying on budget-as-code. It is not exposed for this tenant (404 at sub + tenant scope). Have a Portal fallback. (§4.3)

Enable KVM autostart on any VM providing production services, not just test VMs. A domain controller that does not come back after a host reboot is a single point of failure for the entire AD forest. (§8.2.4)

AAD RBAC grants on AKS can lag the API server by 15+ minutes. If you're verifying cluster access right after a grant, either wait longer or verify at the AAD layer (role assignment) rather than the API-server layer. (§4.5)

The API can return HTTP 200 on a PATCH that does nothing. Always re-read the field you tried to set. Container Insights binding returned 200 but addonProfiles stayed null. (§4.5)

A service principal with UAM cannot revoke its own UAM grant. The ABAC condition on the assignment forbids it. Plan for an external Owner / Admin to perform the final revocation, or disable the SP as an immediate stopgap. (§5.2, §8.1.4)

A frozen replication state on one DC while the other is green is usually a client-side / transport problem, not directory corruption. Verify the services, clear the orphans, run a bounded scoped sync, and only escalate to metadata surgery if the scoped sync still shows failures on a live neighbor. Do not reach for USN rollback or authoritative restore first. (§4.6)

Cost data has a 24–48 h lag. Do not block publishing on actuals — use a retail-rate estimate with an explicit note, and pull actuals as a dated addendum once the lag clears. (§7)

The test of a no-secrets design is not "is there a Key Vault?" — it is "does the Bicep, the repo, the logs, or the write-up contain a secret value?" (§5.3)

Before relying on a terminal's Azure CLI session for privileged operations (especially role-assignment changes), explicitly confirm the active identity via az account show — a session can silently be authenticated as a service principal rather than the intended human account, which is exactly what caused §10.8 to appear unresolvable until the identity mismatch was found. (§10.8)

## 10. Inconsistencies & open items flagged during assembly

These are items the writer flagged rather than silently resolved, per the task's instruction to "flag anything in the source material that seemed inconsistent or unclear."

## 10.1 Deployment-start timestamp discrepancy

PROJECT.md §10.5 states: "deploy 2026-08-25T20:24Z → teardown 2026-08-26."

ops-teardown-abac.log (the ABAC condition createdOn field on the UAM role assignment) states: "2026-08-25T22:33:00.261895+00:00."

verification-report.md Check 5 states: "Deployment start 2026-08-26T01:50:44Z " (this is later than both of the above, which is inconsistent — the verification pass was run on 2026-08-26, so the deployment must have started before that; the 01:50:44Z figure appears to be a different event, possibly the verification pass itself being mislabeled as the "deployment start").

Resolution for this write-up. I used 2026-08-25T22:33Z (the createdOn timestamp on the UAM role assignment, which is the most authoritative single timestamp in the source material — it is the moment the role was granted, which must have been immediately before or during the deploy). The 20:24Z figure from PROJECT.md is 2 h 9 min earlier and may reflect an earlier failed deploy attempt. This is flagged, not silently resolved.

## 10.2 Cost actuals — finalized as a labeled estimate (closed 2026-09-06)

Actual billed cost was not confirmed before publish. The write-up therefore uses a retail-rate estimate (~$25–35 for the ~3-day PoC window, post-gateway-drop) as the final published figure, clearly labeled as an estimate and not a confirmed actual (see §7.3). The original ~$40–55 figure included the VPN gateway line that was dropped on 2026-08-25. This is a labeled estimate, not a guess, and no actual-cost figure is fabricated. The cost-actuals follow-up is closed (see §7.4); cost data remains queryable in Azure Cost Management after the fact should a confirmed figure ever be obtained.

## 10.3 "Resource-visualizer" architecture diagrams do not exist as files

The task instruction was to "include the two architecture diagrams already generated (embed / reference the resource-visualizer images)." No such images exist in the AKS project folder. The only azure-resource-map.png / architecture-diagram.svg files in this box belong to the Domain Controller case study (a different project, in ~/Downloads/ ). The azure-resource-visualizer skill exists in the Cursor plugin cache but was not used to generate any AKS diagrams in this project.

Resolution for this write-up. I generated the two diagrams directly from the authoritative Bicep source ( main.bicep + cluster.bicep ) as Mermaid code blocks (Figure 1 and Figure 2 in §2.1). They are accurate to the source but are newly generated , not "already generated." This is flagged, not fabricated. If the original "resource-visualizer" images exist elsewhere (a different machine, a different folder, a different project), they should be located and substituted.

## 10.4 Task instruction says "2 × D2s_v5" but the source says D2s_v7

The task instruction states: "AKS (2 × D2s_v5 , single namespace)." The actual deployed and verified VM size is Standard_D2s_v7 (see cluster.bicep line 48, main.bicep line 48, and verification-report.md Check 4: "1 pool: node , 2 × Standard_D2s_v7 "). D2s_v5 was not allowed in East US for this subscription (preflight VM size not allowed error, §4.4). This write-up uses D2s_v7 (the real value). This is flagged, not silently "corrected" to match the task instruction.

## 10.5 Task instruction says "single namespace" but the source does not mention namespaces

The task instruction states: "AKS (2 × D2s_v5, single namespace )." The Bicep source and the verification report do not mention a single namespace. The cluster has one node pool ( node , 2 nodes) but the source does not state how many namespaces exist (AKS defaults to default , kube-system , kube-public , kube-node-lease , and any AKS-managed namespaces). This write-up describes the cluster as "single node pool" (the verifiable fact) and does not claim "single namespace." This is flagged, not assumed.

## 10.6 Task instruction says "single database with schemas" but the source does not mention schemas

The task instruction states: "SQL Serverless (centralus, single DB with schemas )." The Bicep source and the verification report confirm a single database ( employeedb ) but do not mention schemas. The portal application (out of scope for this PoC) would define the schemas. This write-up describes it as "single database employeedb " (the verifiable fact) and does not claim "with schemas." This is flagged, not assumed.

## 10.7 SQL Serverless v1 vs v2

cluster.bicep line 365: "SQL (SERVERLESS, General Purpose)" — the comment says v1 (line 366: "At @2021-11-01, Serverless v1 requires: …").

Checkpoint note, line 101: "SQL centralus Serverless v2 (auto-pause 3600s)."

Resolution for this write-up. I used Serverless v1 (the Bicep source is authoritative; the checkpoint is a narrative fragment). This is flagged.

## 10.8 UAM residual step — RESOLVED (manual, by design) — verified 2026-08-27

The User Access Administrator role assignment ( <role-assignment-uam> ) on <deployment-service-principal> has been deleted and independently re-verified . As of 2026-08-27, az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID> --assignee <deployment-service-principal-object-id> returns [] — <deployment-service-principal> holds zero standing role assignments at subscription scope. (The remaining subscription-scope rows are all human Owner assignments — one on the owner MSA plus one on the owner work account. A duplicate Owner row on the owner MSA, created 135 ms after the original by a double-executed grant, was also identified and deleted, leaving exactly two Owner rows.)

Root cause (confirmed, not assumed): the CLI session used for the original revocation attempt was itself authenticated as the <deployment-service-principal> service principal (client ID <deployment-service-principal-client-id> , app-only token), not as a human account. Two deliberate locks made self-resolution impossible for that SP:

Permission gap — Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete is not in the User Access Administrator role definition; UAM grants read + create, not delete. Delete requires Owner .

ABAC self-protection — the assignment additionally carries the by-design GuidNotEquals {<role-def-uam-condition-1>, <role-def-uam-condition-2>, <role-def-uam-condition-3>} condition on write / delete , explicitly excluding its own holder. A deliberate double-lock, not a bug.

Failed autonomous attempt, 2026-08-26 (for continuity with the incident narrative):

HTTP 403 AuthorizationFailed — "The client ' <deployment-service-principal-client-id> ' with object id ' <deployment-service-principal-object-id> ' has an authorization with ABAC condition that is not fulfilled to perform action 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete' over scope …"

Resolution (manual, by the user, under their own Owner account): after identifying that the terminal's active Azure CLI session was unexpectedly authenticated as the SP rather than the user — az account show confirmed the SP was active; an interactive az login switched the session to the human Owner account ( <owner-msa-email> ) — the delete was then run successfully:

az role assignment delete --ids /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/<role-assignment-uam>

Verified via az role assignment list for the assignee returning an empty result ( [] ) — re-run independently by the automation on 2026-08-27 (which was then operating under the human Owner session) with the same empty result.

Note: this was correctly not resolved autonomously by the Hermes agent, per the standing constraint against creating new privileged identities or working around the block — the fix required a genuinely privileged human session, which the automation does not have access to in this environment. This is the intended, safe outcome for this class of exposure, not a shortfall. It closes the last open item from the AKS PoC teardown, and it validates the §8.1.4 anticipation: a SP cannot revoke its own UAM; the final revocation is by design performed by an external human Owner.

## 10.9 Azure Budget object still present

The $300 / month Azure Budget (created manually in the Portal, since ARM 404 for this tenant) is still present at subscription scope after teardown. The PoC cost lines are moot post-teardown, but the budget object itself has not been deleted. This is flagged. If the budget is no longer needed, it should be deleted in the Portal.

— End of case study —

## Contact
To contact AppoSight, use the contact form on the home page: the "Let's build the future together." section (anchor #contact). It asks for your name, your email, an optional phone number, and a short message about your project. The site publishes no public email address, no phone number, and no physical address, and it does not state a response time. The form is the way the site directs visitors to reach the AppoSight team.

## What AppoSight does
AppoSight builds autonomous AI systems ("Intelligence, Reimagined. Building the future of autonomous AI systems."): fine-tuning of language models, AI agents that plan, reason, and execute workflows, model serving and local inference, audio and text-to-speech, model evaluation, and AI penetration testing — autonomous red team operations. The use-case pages describe applied work in identity and access management, Microsoft Entra, Active Directory, and Azure deployments.

## Getting started
Questions about pricing, engagements, or fit are handled through the same contact form on the home page. Include a short description of the project so the AppoSight team can follow up.
